slides.teach: Read the source points, then explain the slide without looking. On Security+, recognition is not enough—you should be able to apply the concept to a scenario.

course.learn: Message-based threat vectors deliver malicious links, attachments, social engineering, or instructions through email, SMS, instant messaging, or collaboration platforms.
course.why: Messaging reaches users directly and can bypass perimeter controls by convincing the user to initiate the unsafe action.
course.example: An attacker sends a fake password-reset link through a collaboration chat rather than email.
course.exam: Do not treat phishing as email-only. The delivery channel may be email, SMS, chat, social media, or another message system.

slides.title: Image, File, and Voice Call
slides.raw:
Image, File, and Voice Call
• Malicious code
• Malicious files
• Vishing
slides.teach: Read the source points, then explain the slide without looking. On Security+, recognition is not enough—you should be able to apply the concept to a scenario.

course.learn: Files, images, documents, and voice calls can all be attack vectors. Files may contain malicious code; media can hide payloads or social-engineering content; voice calls can be used for vishing and impersonation.
course.why: Security controls must inspect both technical content and human manipulation paths.
course.example: A malicious document exploits a vulnerable reader, while a separate caller impersonates IT to request the user's MFA code.
course.exam: Match the vector to the threat: malicious file/code is technical delivery; deceptive voice interaction is vishing/social engineering.

course.learn: Removable devices such as USB drives can carry malware, steal data, bypass network controls, or introduce unauthorized hardware into a system.
course.why: Physical media can cross security boundaries without using normal network paths.
course.example: A found USB drive is plugged into a workstation and automatically launches a malicious payload.
course.exam: Common defenses include device control, disabling autorun, allow listing approved media, encryption, scanning, and user awareness.

course.learn: Vulnerable software contains flaws attackers can identify and exploit to gain access, execute code, escalate privilege, or move deeper into an environment.
course.why: Publicly known vulnerabilities give attackers a repeatable path when organizations delay patching or continue using obsolete software.
course.example: An Internet-facing web framework remains several versions behind and is exploited using a published proof of concept.
course.exam: Inventory, vulnerability scanning, patching, version management, and EOL replacement are the core defensive themes.

breakdown.explanation: The goal is to discover and clearly document the condition so the organization can decide what action to take next.

slides.teach: Build a side-by-side distinction: purpose, strengths, weaknesses, and the scenario where each option fits best.

course.learn: Client-based attacks target software installed on an endpoint, while agentless techniques can interact with services or systems remotely without first installing a local client/agent.
course.why: The distinction changes what prerequisites the attacker needs and where defenders should monitor.
course.example: A malicious document exploits a local office application, while a remote exploit targets an exposed web service directly.
course.exam: Ask whether compromise depends on software running on the victim endpoint or can be performed remotely against an exposed service.

course.learn: Unsupported or end-of-life systems no longer receive normal vendor security fixes, leaving organizations unable to patch newly discovered weaknesses reliably.
course.why: Risk grows over time as new vulnerabilities are found but the product remains unchanged.
course.example: A legacy medical device cannot be upgraded, so it is segmented, tightly monitored, and accessible only through a controlled management path.
course.exam: If replacement is not immediate, use compensating controls such as isolation, allow listing, restricted access, and monitoring.

slides.raw:
Unsecure Networks
Compromising Wi-Fi Networks
Exploiting Wired Networks
Targeting Bluetooth Connections
slides.teach: Read the source points, then explain the slide without looking. On Security+, recognition is not enough—you should be able to apply the concept to a scenario.

course.learn: Unsecure networks expose users to eavesdropping, rogue infrastructure, weak authentication, and traffic manipulation. Public Wi-Fi, poorly configured wired networks, and insecure Bluetooth can all create risk.
course.why: Network proximity can give an attacker a path to observe or influence traffic.
course.example: A traveler uses an open Wi-Fi network; the organization requires a VPN and disables automatic connection to unknown access points.
course.exam: Use authenticated encryption, VPNs, trusted access points, segmentation, and secure wireless configuration.

slides.teach: Read the source points, then explain the slide without looking. On Security+, recognition is not enough—you should be able to apply the concept to a scenario.

course.learn: An open service port means a network service is listening for connections. Every exposed service adds attack surface and must be intentionally required, patched, authenticated, and filtered.
course.why: Attackers scan for exposed services because they provide reachable entry points.
course.example: A server unintentionally exposes a remote-management port to the Internet even though administration should be VPN-only.
course.exam: Close unnecessary ports and restrict necessary management services by firewall, ACL, VPN, or jump host.

slides.raw:
Default Credentials
Using Default Credentials
Neglecting Change

slides.teach: Read the source points, then explain the slide without looking. On Security+, recognition is not enough—you should be able to apply the concept to a scenario.

course.learn: Default credentials are vendor-supplied usernames and passwords that are widely known or easy to discover. Leaving them unchanged gives attackers a predictable authentication path.
course.why: Automated attacks routinely scan for devices still using defaults.
course.example: A newly installed IP camera remains configured with admin/admin and is taken over from the Internet.
course.exam: Changing default credentials is a basic hardening step and should happen before production deployment.

breakdown.explanation: Vendor-supplied usernames/passwords that attackers commonly know and that should be changed before production use.

• Targeting Vendors

slides.teach: Read the source points, then explain the slide without looking. On Security+, recognition is not enough—you should be able to apply the concept to a scenario.

course.learn: A supply-chain attack compromises a trusted supplier, software dependency, hardware component, update mechanism, or service provider so the attacker can reach downstream customers.
course.why: Organizations inherit risk from technology they did not build themselves.
course.example: Attackers compromise a vendor's build environment and malicious code is distributed through a signed software update.
course.exam: Trusted vendor/update/dependency becomes the attack path = supply chain.

slides.teach: Read the source points, then explain the slide without looking. On Security+, recognition is not enough—you should be able to apply the concept to a scenario.

course.learn: Social engineering manipulates people into revealing information, granting access, transferring money, or bypassing procedures. Attackers exploit trust, urgency, authority, fear, curiosity, or helpfulness.
course.why: Technical controls can be bypassed when a legitimate user is persuaded to perform the attacker's action.
course.example: An attacker claims to be a new executive and pressures help desk staff to reset an account outside normal verification procedures.
course.exam: Common forms include phishing, vishing, smishing, impersonation, BEC, watering holes, misinformation, and brand impersonation.

slides.teach: Read the source points, then explain the slide without looking. On Security+, recognition is not enough—you should be able to apply the concept to a scenario.

course.learn: Misinformation is false information shared without necessarily intending harm; disinformation is deliberately false or misleading content intended to influence behavior or perception.
course.why: Manipulating trust and public understanding can support fraud, social engineering, reputational damage, or broader influence operations.
course.example: An attacker deliberately spreads a fake breach notice using copied company branding to drive customers to a credential-stealing site.
course.exam: The important distinction is intent: disinformation is intentionally deceptive; misinformation may be inaccurate without malicious intent.

course.learn: Impersonation pretends to be a trusted person or organization to gain information, access, money, or credibility. Brand impersonation copies logos, domains, websites, or communication style to appear legitimate.
course.why: People make trust decisions quickly based on familiar names and appearance.
course.example: A fake support account uses the company logo and a look-alike domain to send customers to a malicious sign-in page.
course.exam: Verify identity through trusted channels; look-alike domains and copied branding are strong clues.

breakdown.explanation: Social engineering manipulates people into revealing information, granting access, transferring money, or bypassing procedures. Attackers exploit trust, urgency, authority, fear, curiosity, or helpfulness.

slides.teach: Read the source points, then explain the slide without looking. On Security+, recognition is not enough—you should be able to apply the concept to a scenario.

course.learn: Business Email Compromise (BEC) is a targeted fraud in which attackers impersonate or take over a trusted business identity to manipulate payments, invoices, payroll, or sensitive data.
course.why: BEC can cause large financial losses without malware if the social deception is convincing.
course.example: An attacker compromises a vendor mailbox and sends a real customer an invoice with new bank details.
course.exam: Look for executive/vendor impersonation, wire-transfer requests, invoice changes, and urgent financial action.

course.learn: A watering-hole attack compromises a website frequently visited by the intended victims so the attacker can reach them indirectly.
course.why: Targeting a trusted site can bypass users' suspicion of unsolicited links.
course.example: An attacker compromises an industry association website that employees of several target companies visit every day.
course.exam: Targeted victims + compromised site they normally visit = watering hole.

slides.teach: Read the source points, then explain the slide without looking. On Security+, recognition is not enough—you should be able to apply the concept to a scenario.

course.learn: Typosquatting registers look-alike domain names based on common typing mistakes or visually similar characters so victims land on an attacker-controlled site.
course.why: Users may overlook small domain differences, allowing credential theft or malware delivery.
course.example: micros0ft-support.example is designed to resemble a legitimate brand domain.
course.exam: Misspelled/look-alike domain = typosquatting. Broader copying of a company identity is brand impersonation.
